MiniWireshark **5.3.4**: a medium release that makes MiniWireshark safer, easier to start and easier to understand.

**Security and privacy**
- Every finding of the 5.2.3 security audit is fixed in the code. Four still need a check on real hardware (a Windows PC, a Mac, a real Wi-Fi roam).
- Linux and macOS no longer start as administrator. The password is asked for only when capture starts, and the demo and the help never ask.
- The data folder is closed to other users. Another user can no longer swap the compiled copy, the update rollback or the private packages.
- A new install no longer trusts its first network or starts Active Scanning by itself. "Session only" and "Delete ALL history" really delete.
- Passwords stay out of packet details, saved conversations, CSV files and copies. A new warning says when a login is sent without encryption, without keeping the password.
- A second device claiming to be the router raises a DANGER alert. The kill switch also stops package downloads.

**New**
- **Ready?** in the Welcome Center: what works, and a fix button for what doesn't.
- **Story mode** in the Timeline: what changed, day by day, in plain sentences.
- **Unusual activity** in the Security tab, with the worrying and the innocent reading side by side, and a day-and-night baseline for each device.
- **Seven guided questions**, among them DNS, IPv6, "can't connect", "Wi-Fi or Internet?" and call problems.
- **Calls**: loss and jitter of video and voice calls, from packet headers only.
- **Network check-up**: one plain-English page to print or send, names hidden by default.
- Alert snooze, your own blocklist, opt-in notifications while minimised, `--help` and `--version`, and a filter said in words.

**Speed and fixes**
- Windows now starts from the saved compiled copy too: on a Windows PC the first start went from about 14 to under 5 seconds, and memory from about 440 to about 220 MB.
- Packets are analysed about a fifth faster, and memory stays flatter over long runs.
- Damaged files, clocks that jump, German and Windows 11 24H2 Wi-Fi output, and every layout from 1024×768 up in three languages are handled.

**Known limits**
- **Changing the text size on Windows is slow.** It takes about 0.4 seconds on the test machine, and the window doesn't answer for about a tenth of a second while it happens (the goal is 0.1 seconds; on Linux it is well under that). The reason: on Windows every part of the window is its own small system window, and when the shared fonts change, all of them (about 700) are measured and drawn again. Making this fast needs a change to how the window shares its fonts, planned for a later release.
- **Not re-tested on a real PC for this release: long-run memory, thread and handle growth on Windows, and the network-card pick with a VPN connected.** The last real 8-hour run was on an older build. On that build memory grew by about 8–9 MB an hour, Python threads went from 13 to 19, system threads from 15 to 24 and handles from 318 to 507. Changes made since then are meant to stop this growth: each background job runs only one at a time, a helper program that hangs is ended together with anything it started, and finished helper programs are closed properly. These changes are checked by automated tests on Linux only, not on a Windows PC, so this is untested, not fixed. The evidence that does exist is the GUI test step "round 8: 500 rounds of the periodic jobs in fast time" (`gt_r8_long_run_fast_time`). It runs the network check, capture start, stop and restart, the programs table, the Wi-Fi check, the update check and the screen refresh 500 times, with helpers that hang, fail or are slow. It then checks that threads, open files and helper processes are back to where they started. It uses a fake capture in place of Npcap, and it does not show how memory behaves over hours. The soak script (`.github/scripts/soak.py`) replays saved packets and never opens Npcap, so it does not cover live capture either. Its "blocks" figure counts memory blocks handed out by Python's small-object allocator (pymalloc), not objects.

**Quality**
- Self-test 272/272 on Python 3.8 and 3.12.
- GUI test 62/62.
- A million damaged packets in a row, 0 errors.
